caption:
Your content’s analytics are telling you what’s missing from your content strategy👀

Here’s how to read them and what to do with them.

If your content gets low views but high engagement, that usually means the idea is resonating with the people who see it, but the packaging isn’t strong enough to reach more people.

The message may be good, but the angle, spoken/text hook, visual hook, or first few seconds are not making a wide enough group of people stop.

That’s when you need to package the idea to get the most people to find it interesting.

If your content gets high views but low engagement, usually the problem isn’t attention, it’s that people didn’t feel emotionally connected enough to respond.

That usually means the content needs to speak more directly to your audience’s desires, fears, frustrations, problems, beliefs, or experiences.

Because when people see themselves in your content, they want to weigh in on the conversation, share it with someone, or save it for later.

If your content gets low views and low engagement, it’s usually because the topic is too generic, too obvious, too broad, or too disconnected from what your audience actually cares about.

Go back to what your real clients ask, the mistakes they make, their fears, etc and make content about that. And if you don’t have clients yet, see what people are searching for in your industry on the internet.

Now if your content gets high views, high engagement, but low leads, that means that people are resonating with your content, but they don’t clearly understand what problem you solve, what results you’ve helped people get, or why they should trust you specifically.

And when those things are unclear, people consume your content without connecting it back to your business. People need to see proof that you have the solution to their specific problems, you know what you’re doing, and you are THE person to help them.

Combine all those things, and you’ve got a solid content strategy :)

caption:
How did such a simple hack get over 1.3 million views?

It comes down to the psychology of what makes us pay attention and want to share with others. 

Here are a few ways you can use this for your content:

You can start with something visual that looks wrong, broken, or irreversible. 

You can say something that sounds like a confession or mistake. 

Or you can do something that makes the viewer go “wait what did they just do?!”

Then you let the rest of your video show the resolution.

A few examples:

Car detailing: show a before that looks completely irreparable, and then show how you fix it

Nutritionist: start eating something unexpected on camera, then explain why you approve of it

Artist: ‘destroy’ your art before showing that that’s part of your creative process

Florist: Show a completely wilted, dead-looking bouquet, then bring it fully back to life on camera

Financial advisor: “I just moved everything out of the market” – then show exactly why, and what you moved it into

Just remember that these videos can be great for views and engagement, but if you want to grow your business on social media, make sure you’re balancing these out with content that shows your expertise and builds connection with your audience.

caption:
Comment "Day 2" to get my full prompt vocabulary guide — the exact language that makes AI output look shot, not generated. 

What you're seeing was shot on IMAX. 

That's what I'd say if I was a liar. 

This was made entirely with AI. 

So why does it look real and natural instead of the default slop flooding your feed? Three things. Almost nobody does all three. 

First — stop using one model for everything. 

The single fastest way into slop territory is forcing one model to do a job it was never built for. 

Realism → Soul 2.0. Cinematic frames → Soul Cinema. Text-heavy images → GPT 2.0. General editing → Nano Banana 2.0. 

Right model, right job. That alone fixes half the problem. 

Second — prompt like you're on set with an infinite budget. 

Name the camera. Name the lens. Name the director whose eye you want. Name the film the shot should feel like. 

The model doesn't guess what "cinematic" means. It renders what you can actually name. 

Which is the real bottleneck — not the tool, your vocabulary. Most people are describing a scene with maybe twenty words of film language. A cinematographer has thousands. 

Third — add organic texture on top. 

Film grain. Halation. Bloom. 

AI output is too clean. No sensor noise, no lens imperfection, nothing a real camera would have introduced. That sterility is what your eye reads as fake before you can explain why. 

Put the imperfection back and it stops looking rendered. Dehancer if you want the proper film emulation, or just an overlay in Premiere if you want it in thirty seconds. 

Think of it like post on a real film. The footage is never the final look. The grade and the grain are what make it cinema. 

What changes when you run all three: 

1. Output that reads as shot, not generated 
2. A repeatable look instead of one lucky render 
3. Work that survives a second look on a big screen 

For anyone making stylized shorts, brand films, or cinematic sequences with AI — this is the difference between a clip and a frame that holds.

principles.rule: Position all critical on-screen text and key visual elements strictly within safe zones that remain completely clear of native platform interactive overlays, such as like, comment, share, and profile buttons.
principles.why: Placing essential content beneath interactive platform elements causes visual clutter, renders text unreadable, and leads to accidental triggers of platform actions when users attempt to read or interact with the content.
principles.example: Before: Placing captions in the bottom-right corner of a vertical video where they are obscured by the Instagram 'Like' and 'Comment' icons. principles.rule: Synchronize kinetic text animations to trigger precisely on the exact frame of the corresponding spoken word or audio beat, avoiding loose approximations.
principles.why: Tight alignment between auditory and visual stimuli reduces cognitive processing lag, enhances reading comprehension, and creates a highly polished, immersive user experience.
principles.example: Before: Captions appearing with a loose delay after the speaker says a word, causing a jarring visual lag. After: Captions rendering instantly on the exact frame the audio waveform peaks for each spoken word.

caption:
I grew this channel from 0 to $100K in revenue in my first 3 months.

This is the exact content production system I ran to post 99 times in my first 100 days.

Step 1 is to batch ideation.

I run this Claude skill with the Sandcastles MCP to automatically analyze all the top outliers in my niche.

It runs every morning and it builds this Notion database sorted by performance.

Now the goal is not to copy these.

The goal is to aim my creativity towards topics that have already worked.

I start at the top, watch each video, and decide if I have anything new and interesting to say.

If I don’t, I skip. If I do, it makes the shortlist.

Once I have 7 videos on the shortlist, I move to step 2.

Step 2 is scriptwriting.

I don’t use AI for writing, I think it waters down everything.

I open a google doc, and ask myself, “What would be the most valuable thing I could share about this topic for my ideal viewer?”

A business owner making content trying to grow their business.

Typically it’s a breakdown, how-to or list of instructions for implementing a framework.

I write those down as compressed as possible and that’s my script.

For the hook, I look at a list of all my best previous hooks and loosely model the new one as best I can.

I write all my scripts in one session. This takes about 3 hours.

Step 3 is recording.

I then batch record all 7 videos in a single session. Takes about 45 minutes end to end.

Step 4, I upload the raw files into folders and send them to my editing team.

They edit all of the videos and send them back when ready. 

And I post them daily.

Step 5, we take all the best performing videos and turn them into carousels 30-60 days later.

And that’s the whole process.

4 hours per week, 0 to 60K followers, 30,000 emails and $100K in revenue in the first 3 months.
